title: SCS Release and Deployment Management
text:
This section defines how ngGONG Station Control System (SCS) build artifacts are identified, assembled into SCS releases, qualified, promoted, deployed, revoked, rolled back, and retained. The process applies to the SCS and can be adapted for other software systems.
The process separates four concepts that must not be conflated:

Build identity identifies the output of one component build.
Artifact identity identifies immutable artifact content, such as a container-image digest.
Release identity identifies one tested composition of component artifacts and deployment configuration.
Deployment state identifies the release currently approved for a channel or station.

Container images and release manifests are immutable. Names such as candidate, production, and station-specific deployment channels are mutable pointers to immutable objects.



Source code shall be maintained in Git repositories. Build artifacts shall be published to repositories designed for their artifact type rather than committed to Git.

Reusable libraries (e.g. a Java .jar) shall be published to an artifact repository (e.g. Maven) when another component consumes them as dependencies.
Deployable services shall be published as container images to a container registry.
A service does not need a separately published library unless another component consumes that library.
System release manifests shall be stored as immutable release artifacts in the SCS deployment repository, such as assets attached to GitHub Releases.

Artifact versioning shall reflect how the artifact is consumed:

Reusable libraries that are selected independently by downstream builds shall use Semantic Versions.
Deployable applications and their container images shall use CI-generated build identifiers rather than Semantic Versions.
Interface and schema versions shall be managed independently when consumers need explicit compatibility information.
The deployed SCS shall be versioned through its release manifest rather than through a shared application version.

An application build identifier shall be generated entirely by CI. Developers shall not edit or increment it in source. A format similar to the following is recommended:
<UTC-date>.<CI-run-id>.<run-attempt>
For example:
20261007.4387291542.1
The date provides human context, the CI run ID provides repository-scoped uniqueness, and the attempt distinguishes reruns that could produce different artifacts. The exact field definitions shall be documented for the selected CI system.
The source revision and creation time shall instead be recorded as structured artifact metadata, including the applicable OCI annotations:
org.opencontainers.image.version
org.opencontainers.image.created
org.opencontainers.image.revision
org.opencontainers.image.source
Human-readable tags may be used for navigation, but deployment decisions shall use immutable container-image digests. A tag such as candidate may move when a newer eligible build becomes available; a digest such as sha256:abc123... identifies fixed content.


Reusable libraries, including JARs generated from shared Protocol Buffer definitions, shall use Semantic Versions. The compatibility policy for each library shall define what constitutes a major, minor, or patch change. For a shared Protocol Buffer library, the default policy is:

incompatible wire, generated-API, or defined semantic changes require a major increment;
backward-compatible additions to the published interface require a minor increment; and
compatible corrections that do not add published interface surface require a patch increment.

Automated schema-compatibility checks shall verify that a breaking change is not published without the required version transition. A major version increment labels a compatibility break; it does not replace the migration or coexistence plan needed by deployed consumers.
Official library versions shall be immutable and shall be derived from, or verified against, protected Git release tags. Release-tag protection shall restrict creation to authorized identities and prevent modification or deletion after publication. Whether release tags must also be cryptographically signed, and which identities may create them, remain TBD. The source POM may use Maven CI-friendly version placeholders so normal development does not require developers to edit a shared version field. Release automation shall resolve the placeholder to the approved Semantic Version when it publishes the library.
Pull-request and local-development artifacts may use versions such as:
0.0.0-pr.417-SNAPSHOT
0.0.0-local-SNAPSHOT
These versions are temporary integration aids. They shall not be referenced by the main branch of a consuming application, included in an SCS release manifest, or deployed to production. Application repositories shall have a required merge check that rejects temporary and snapshot dependencies.
The CI pipeline shall verify externally sourced dependencies and build inputs against the project’s software supply-chain acceptance policy before publishing component artifacts. Verification results shall be associated with the published artifacts.
Published artifacts should include, when supported by the build and registry infrastructure:

the source commit identifier;
build and dependency metadata;
a software bill of materials (SBOM);
provenance or build attestations; and
vulnerability-scan results or a reference to the applicable scan record.





The Developer Guide describes the cross-repository library change workflow and its proposed GitHub automation.
Each deployable component shall have its own CI pipeline. The pipeline shall, at minimum:

compile and package the component;
run unit and component tests;
run static analysis and other required quality and security checks;
verify applicable API, message-schema, and interface contracts;
build the container image;
publish the image under a unique build identifier; and
resolve and record the published image digest.

The application build identifier shall be injected by CI. It shall not be committed to the application source tree. The component image shall record the exact released versions of its reusable dependencies in its build metadata or SBOM.
After these checks pass, the component’s candidate channel may be advanced to the new image digest. At the component level, candidate means only that the artifact passed its own CI and is eligible for inclusion in a system release candidate. It does not mean that the component has passed SCS system testing or is approved for production.
Interface changes should be additive by default. Breaking changes shall use an explicit interface-version transition and, when practical, an expand-and-contract sequence that permits old and new component versions to coexist during deployment. Exhaustive pairwise old/new integration testing is not required for every component build. Fast contract and schema-compatibility checks shall protect service boundaries in component CI, while assembled-system tests shall run against a fixed SCS composition.



A dedicated SCS deployment repository shall define deployment configuration and create system release candidates. On a scheduled trigger (daily), or on an authorized manual trigger, its release-composition pipeline shall:

identify the current eligible candidate for each required SCS component;
resolve every candidate tag or channel to an immutable image digest;
identify the exact deployment-configuration revision;
generate an immutable SCS release manifest;
assign the manifest a unique SCS release identifier;
archive the manifest before deployment;
advance the SCS candidate channel to the new release identifier; and
request deployment of that release to the test environment.

The pipeline shall fail rather than create an incomplete manifest when a required component cannot be resolved or its provenance cannot be verified.
An SCS release identifier may use a date and sequence number, for example:
2026.09.01.01
Once assigned, a release identifier shall never be reused for different content.


The release manifest is the system-level release artifact. It declares the exact content that was tested; it is not a copy of the component images. At minimum, it shall record:

the SCS release identifier;
the creation time and creating pipeline run;
the source revision of the deployment repository;
every component name, image location, image digest, build identifier, and source revision;
the deployment-configuration revision;
applicable configuration-schema and database-migration levels;
references to SBOMs, attestations, and other provenance records where available; and
manifest format or schema version.

For example:
schema_version: 1
release: 2026.09.01.01
created: 2026-09-01T22:00:00Z
deployment_revision: 71bd8af

components:
  acquisition:
    image: ghcr.io/nggong/scs-acquisition@sha256:aaa...
    build: 20260901.4387291542.1
    source_revision: 4f92ac1

  sa:
    image: ghcr.io/nggong/scs-sa@sha256:bbb...
    build: 20260901.4387291668.1
    source_revision: ab12c34

  transfer:
    image: ghcr.io/nggong/scs-transfer@sha256:ccc...
    build: 20260901.4387292017.1
    source_revision: 9981def

configuration:
  schema: 3
  database_migration: 17
The manifest schema shall be machine-validated. Its canonical content should also be signed or covered by a repository or release attestation.




The test environment shall consume the SCS candidate channel and deploy the exact release manifest referenced by that channel. It shall not independently select the latest component images.
System qualification shall include the applicable integration, system, operational, upgrade, and regression tests. Qualification results shall be associated with the exact SCS release identifier and manifest digest. New component candidates published while qualification is in progress shall not alter the release under test; they are eligible only for a later composition.
If qualification fails:

the release shall not be promoted;
the failed manifest and results shall be retained for traceability;
the SCS candidate channel may advance to a later corrected release; and
no component image or release manifest shall be changed in place.

If qualification succeeds, an authorized promotion workflow shall advance the production channel to the qualified release identifier. The workflow shall promote the same manifest and image digests that passed testing. It shall not rebuild the component images or generate a replacement manifest.
Promotion is therefore a deployment-state change:
candidate  -> 2026.09.01.02
production -> 2026.09.01.01
It is not a change to the artifacts referenced by either release.



A deployment channel is a mutable, version-controlled pointer to an immutable release manifest. The deployment repository or an NSO-controlled deployment service derived from it shall be the authoritative source of channel state.
The project shall not use GitHub’s latest release designation, a container latest tag, or lexicographic sorting of release names as the production-approval mechanism. Stations shall request the release explicitly approved for their applicable channel.
The channel model should allow a global production release and controlled exceptions, for example:
production:
  release: 2026.09.01.01

station_overrides:
  mauna-loa:
    release: 2026.08.29.01
    reason: maintenance-hold

revoked:
  - release: 2026.08.30.01
    reason: NGGONG-1234
Changes to production and station-specific channels shall be authenticated, authorized, auditable, and recoverable through version history. Normal promotion should use the standard review process. A documented emergency process shall permit an authorized operator to revoke or roll back a release without waiting for the normal release schedule.



At each scheduled deployment opportunity, the station shall retrieve current channel and revocation state from the authoritative source to determine whether a deployment is authorized. The deployment state shall be signed or authenticated. The station shall not retain a pending deployment request for execution at a later opportunity without repeating that check. A station deployment agent shall:

retrieve the release approved for the station’s applicable channel;
retrieve the current revocation state;
determine whether the release approved for that station differs from the locally installed release;
verify the release manifest, provenance, and referenced image digests;
stage required artifacts without changing the running system, where practical;
deploy during a locally appropriate operational window;
run required post-deployment health checks; and
report and retain the installed release identifier and deployment result.

Stations shall deploy only artifacts named by the approved release manifest. They shall not follow component-level candidate, production, or latest tags.
Station deployment shall verify current release authorization and confirm that retrieved artifacts match the identities recorded in the approved release manifest. Stations are not required to repeat the supply-chain checks performed by CI.
Detailed cybersecurity controls, acceptance criteria, credential management, and any signing or attestation requirements remain TBD and shall be defined through the project’s cybersecurity design process.
A station shall not deploy solely from a stale cached production pointer. Before starting a deployment, it shall confirm that the selected release remains approved and is not revoked. If current authorization state cannot be obtained, the default behavior shall be to keep the installed release rather than begin a new deployment. The project shall define any controlled exception needed for extended network outages.
Revocation prevents subsequent deployment attempts. If revocation occurs after a deployment has begun, engineering personnel shall assess affected stations and direct rollback or other recovery when appropriate.
A deployment attempt shall have a recorded outcome identifying the target release and the component versions actually running. If deployment or post-deployment checks fail, the station shall not resume normal observing until it has reached a qualified configuration or an explicitly authorized recovery state. Recovery may involve a rollback to the last known good release for the station.



Promotion, revocation, and rollback are separate operations:

Promotion advances a deployment channel to a newly qualified release.
Revocation declares that a release must not receive future deployments.
Rollback changes desired or installed state to a prior known-good release.

If a production release is found to be defective after one or more stations deploy it, the incident response shall:

mark the affected release as revoked and record the reason and incident reference;
move the production channel to the last known-good release;
publish the updated channel and revocation state immediately;
identify stations that downloaded, staged, or installed the revoked release;
direct affected stations to roll back when rollback is safe;
preserve the revoked release manifest, images, evidence, and deployment history;
correct the affected component through its normal build pipeline; and
compose and fully qualify a new SCS release.

The revoked release shall not be deleted or modified. Its release notes or external status metadata may identify it as revoked, but its tag, manifest, and attached artifacts shall remain unchanged.
For a GitHub-based implementation, immutable GitHub Releases may hold the release manifests. Mutable channel and revocation state should remain as version-controlled files or be published by a deployment service. An emergency rollback changes channels/production.yaml to the previous release and adds the defective release to the revocation record. The change is then committed, reviewed under the emergency procedure, merged, and published to stations. GitHub’s latest release indicator shall not be treated as the channel pointer.
Rollback shall not be assumed to be safe for stateful components. Database migrations, persisted data formats, protocol state, and external controller configuration can prevent a simple return to old containers. Each stateful component shall declare one of the following for every release transition:

rollback to the previous production release is supported;
rollback requires restoration of identified state or data; or
rollback is not supported and recovery requires a forward fix.

Irreversible migrations require an approved recovery plan before promotion.



Artifact pruning shall be based on reachability and operational need, not only artifact age.
The retention process shall protect:

every artifact referenced by a candidate, production, station-specific, or other active channel;
every artifact referenced by an immutable release manifest retained under the project records policy;
the release currently installed or staged at each station;
at least the configured number of prior known-good releases needed for rollback;
revoked releases and artifacts required for incident analysis; and
artifacts subject to a legal, security, audit, or milestone hold.

Unreferenced component candidates that never entered a release manifest may be deleted after a defined grace period. Temporary build products and CI logs may use shorter retention periods if they are not required to reproduce or audit a release. Registry garbage collection shall run only after the reachability calculation and grace period are complete.
Temporary Maven artifacts published for pull-request integration shall use a distinct version pattern and retention policy. They may be removed after their source pull requests are closed and no open consumer pull request references them. Published Semantic Version releases shall not be overwritten or removed merely because they are no longer selected by current applications.
Deleting a mutable tag does not necessarily delete image content, and deleting image content can break an old release even when its manifest remains. The pruning process shall therefore work from immutable digests and shall verify that no protected manifest or deployed station references an artifact before deletion.
Retention durations, the rollback depth, and the treatment of milestone releases shall be defined in the project records and configuration-management policies. These values remain TBD until those policies are approved.



The release process shall make it possible to determine:

which source revisions produced each component artifact;
which artifact digests formed each SCS release;
which deployment configuration was applied;
which tests qualified the release and their results;
who or what promoted, revoked, or rolled back the release;
which release each station installed and when; and
whether deployment and post-deployment checks succeeded.

Release, channel, test, and station-deployment records shall use stable identifiers so that records can be correlated across Git, CI, artifact registries, the deployment service, and observability systems.



Specific organizational assignments remain TBD, but the following responsibilities shall be assigned:

Component maintainers maintain component CI, interface contracts, artifact metadata, and component rollback declarations.
Release automation composes and validates immutable SCS release manifests.
Test authority defines qualification criteria and accepts or rejects a release candidate.
Release authority approves production promotion and emergency channel changes.
Station operations control local deployment windows and respond to failed deployments.
Configuration management maintains release records, retention rules, and auditability.

No single mutable tag or unrecorded runtime state shall be the only evidence of what was tested, approved, or deployed.

title: SCS Release and Deployment Management
text:
This section defines how ngGONG Station Control System (SCS) build artifacts are identified, assembled into SCS releases, qualified, promoted, deployed, revoked, rolled back, and retained. The process applies to the SCS and can be adapted for other software systems.
The process separates four concepts that must not be conflated:

Build identity identifies the output of one component build.
Artifact identity identifies immutable artifact content, such as a container-image digest.
Release identity identifies one tested composition of component artifacts and deployment configuration.
Deployment state identifies the release currently approved for a channel or station.

Container images and release manifests are immutable. Names such as candidate, production, and station-specific deployment channels are mutable pointers to immutable objects.

title: SCS Release and Deployment Management
text:
Source code shall be maintained in Git repositories. Build artifacts shall be published to repositories designed for their artifact type rather than committed to Git.

Reusable libraries (e.g. a Java .jar) shall be published to an artifact repository (e.g. Maven) when another component consumes them as dependencies.
Deployable services shall be published as container images to a container registry.
A service does not need a separately published library unless another component consumes that library.
System release manifests shall be stored as immutable release artifacts in the SCS deployment repository, such as assets attached to GitHub Releases.

Artifact versioning shall reflect how the artifact is consumed:

Reusable libraries that are selected independently by downstream builds shall use Semantic Versions.
Deployable applications and their container images shall use CI-generated build identifiers rather than Semantic Versions.
Interface and schema versions shall be managed independently when consumers need explicit compatibility information.
The deployed SCS shall be versioned through its release manifest rather than through a shared application version.

An application build identifier shall be generated entirely by CI. Developers shall not edit or increment it in source. A format similar to the following is recommended:
<UTC-date>.<CI-run-id>.<run-attempt>
For example:
20261007.4387291542.1
The date provides human context, the CI run ID provides repository-scoped uniqueness, and the attempt distinguishes reruns that could produce different artifacts. The exact field definitions shall be documented for the selected CI system.
The source revision and creation time shall instead be recorded as structured artifact metadata, including the applicable OCI annotations:
org.opencontainers.image.version
org.opencontainers.image.created
org.opencontainers.image.revision
org.opencontainers.image.source
Human-readable tags may be used for navigation, but deployment decisions shall use immutable container-image digests. A tag such as candidate may move when a newer eligible build becomes available; a digest such as sha256:abc123... identifies fixed content.


Reusable libraries, including JARs generated from shared Protocol Buffer definitions, shall use Semantic Versions. The compatibility policy for each library shall define what constitutes a major, minor, or patch change. For a shared Protocol Buffer library, the default policy is:

incompatible wire, generated-API, or defined semantic changes require a major increment;
backward-compatible additions to the published interface require a minor increment; and
compatible corrections that do not add published interface surface require a patch increment.

Automated schema-compatibility checks shall verify that a breaking change is not published without the required version transition. A major version increment labels a compatibility break; it does not replace the migration or coexistence plan needed by deployed consumers.
Official library versions shall be immutable and shall be derived from, or verified against, protected Git release tags. Release-tag protection shall restrict creation to authorized identities and prevent modification or deletion after publication. Whether release tags must also be cryptographically signed, and which identities may create them, remain TBD. The source POM may use Maven CI-friendly version placeholders so normal development does not require developers to edit a shared version field. Release automation shall resolve the placeholder to the approved Semantic Version when it publishes the library.
Pull-request and local-development artifacts may use versions such as:
0.0.0-pr.417-SNAPSHOT
0.0.0-local-SNAPSHOT
These versions are temporary integration aids. They shall not be referenced by the main branch of a consuming application, included in an SCS release manifest, or deployed to production. Application repositories shall have a required merge check that rejects temporary and snapshot dependencies.
The CI pipeline shall verify externally sourced dependencies and build inputs against the project’s software supply-chain acceptance policy before publishing component artifacts. Verification results shall be associated with the published artifacts.
Published artifacts should include, when supported by the build and registry infrastructure:

the source commit identifier;
build and dependency metadata;
a software bill of materials (SBOM);
provenance or build attestations; and
vulnerability-scan results or a reference to the applicable scan record.

title: SCS Release and Deployment Management
SCS Release and Deployment Management
text:
A dedicated SCS deployment repository shall define deployment configuration and create system release candidates. On a scheduled trigger (daily), or on an authorized manual trigger, its release-composition pipeline shall:

identify the current eligible candidate for each required SCS component;
resolve every candidate tag or channel to an immutable image digest;
identify the exact deployment-configuration revision;
generate an immutable SCS release manifest;
assign the manifest a unique SCS release identifier;
archive the manifest before deployment;
advance the SCS candidate channel to the new release identifier; and
request deployment of that release to the test environment.

The pipeline shall fail rather than create an incomplete manifest when a required component cannot be resolved or its provenance cannot be verified.
An SCS release identifier may use a date and sequence number, for example:
2026.09.01.01
Once assigned, a release identifier shall never be reused for different content.


The release manifest is the system-level release artifact. It declares the exact content that was tested; it is not a copy of the component images. At minimum, it shall record:

the SCS release identifier;
the creation time and creating pipeline run;
the source revision of the deployment repository;
every component name, image location, image digest, build identifier, and source revision;
the deployment-configuration revision;
applicable configuration-schema and database-migration levels;
references to SBOMs, attestations, and other provenance records where available; and
manifest format or schema version.

For example:
schema_version: 1
release: 2026.09.01.01
created: 2026-09-01T22:00:00Z
deployment_revision: 71bd8af

components:
  acquisition:
    image: ghcr.io/nggong/scs-acquisition@sha256:aaa...
    build: 20260901.4387291542.1
    source_revision: 4f92ac1

  sa:
    image: ghcr.io/nggong/scs-sa@sha256:bbb...
    build: 20260901.4387291668.1
    source_revision: ab12c34

  transfer:
    image: ghcr.io/nggong/scs-transfer@sha256:ccc...
    build: 20260901.4387292017.1
    source_revision: 9981def

configuration:
  schema: 3
  database_migration: 17
The manifest schema shall be machine-validated. Its canonical content should also be signed or covered by a repository or release attestation.

title: SCS Release and Deployment Management
text:
The test environment shall consume the SCS candidate channel and deploy the exact release manifest referenced by that channel. It shall not independently select the latest component images.
System qualification shall include the applicable integration, system, operational, upgrade, and regression tests. Qualification results shall be associated with the exact SCS release identifier and manifest digest. New component candidates published while qualification is in progress shall not alter the release under test; they are eligible only for a later composition.
If qualification fails:

the release shall not be promoted;
the failed manifest and results shall be retained for traceability;
the SCS candidate channel may advance to a later corrected release; and
no component image or release manifest shall be changed in place.

If qualification succeeds, an authorized promotion workflow shall advance the production channel to the qualified release identifier. The workflow shall promote the same manifest and image digests that passed testing. It shall not rebuild the component images or generate a replacement manifest.
Promotion is therefore a deployment-state change:
candidate  -> 2026.09.01.02
production -> 2026.09.01.01
It is not a change to the artifacts referenced by either release.

title: SCS Release and Deployment Management
text:
A deployment channel is a mutable, version-controlled pointer to an immutable release manifest. The deployment repository or an NSO-controlled deployment service derived from it shall be the authoritative source of channel state.
The project shall not use GitHub’s latest release designation, a container latest tag, or lexicographic sorting of release names as the production-approval mechanism. Stations shall request the release explicitly approved for their applicable channel.
The channel model should allow a global production release and controlled exceptions, for example:
production:
  release: 2026.09.01.01

station_overrides:
  mauna-loa:
    release: 2026.08.29.01
    reason: maintenance-hold

revoked:
  - release: 2026.08.30.01
    reason: NGGONG-1234
Changes to production and station-specific channels shall be authenticated, authorized, auditable, and recoverable through version history. Normal promotion should use the standard review process. A documented emergency process shall permit an authorized operator to revoke or roll back a release without waiting for the normal release schedule.
